spec_choices.why: The designer chose 4. The minimum is 3 because with 2 players there is little contest over lots and almost nothing to hide a Favourite among. The maximum is 4 because the deck and the Favourite set (four Favourites) are built for at most 4.
The source has no negotiation. Picks are public, and the interest lies in reading others' Favourites from their picks and hate-drafting, so talk would only add words.

A thoughtful player balances food against cats to avoid unfed cats and the food penalty, chases toy sets and catnip, and infers rivals' secret Favourites from what they take so as to deny them key lots.

variation.original_summary: Cat Lady is a 2-4 player card-drafting game. Players take rows or columns from a 3x3 market of cards and collect cats that must be fed with food, plus toys (scored in sets), catnip (scored on an increasing scale), stray cats and other cards. Highest victory points wins. The previously reviewed variation replaced the grid with a market of 2-card lots drafted in rotating seat order, and added one secret Favourite per player.

review.evidence: No simple policy wins. 'Always earliest letter' and 'always latest letter' take effectively random lots, collect unfed cats at -1 and attract the food penalty, so they lose to a greedy drafter. 'Always most catnip' splits 16 cards with any other chaser and ignores Strays. 'Always most points now' ignores feeding dependencies. However, the 4-player game ran 9 rounds, so seat 1 picked first 3 times and last 2 times while seat 4 did the reverse. Picking first from 5 lots instead of last from 2 is worth about 2-4 points, which gave seat 1 an edge of about 4-8 points in totals of 40-60. That is a built-in seat edge.

Lot contents are public before anyone picks. Values depend on what a player already holds (food against cats, toy colours, the catnip curve) and on what rivals need. The skilled drafter plans feeding, completes sets and hate-drafts. Randomness lies only in which lots appear, and every player faces the same market.

A weak player still scores through Strays (3 flat) and loose toys. A strong player can keep improving through timing, denial and reading Favourites from rivals' picks. Food scarcity (38 food for 20 cats) makes feeding a real planning problem.

Each player's secret Favourite changes what they value, so players must infer rivals' Favourites from their picks to predict and deny. Planning across rounds matters for feeding, the catnip curve and toy sets. The Favourite gap was a minor lottery element: Cats was worth about +10-12 and Catnip about +6-7.
Every score is arithmetic on public counts plus a revealed Favourite. The winner and tie-break are numeric.
The game is text-only, sequential picks are turn-based, and there is no board. It uses one hidden element, one market deal per round, at most 4 choice steps per round and at most 12 rounds.

problems: P1: In the 4-player game, 9 rounds cannot be split evenly over 4 seats. Seat 1 picks first 3 times and last 2 times while seat 4 does the reverse, a structural edge of about 4-8 points.
P2: Favourite bonuses are uneven (Cats about +10-12, Toys about +8-10, Catnip about +6-7, Strays about +6-8), so the secret deal tilts the result before skill acts.
P3: Because the deck is used differently at 4 players, the Favourite values need re-checking against how many Catnip and Stray cards actually appear.

changes.what: The 4-player game becomes 8 rounds of 5 lots of 2 cards (80 of the 96 cards are dealt; the bottom 16 are never used). The first picker still rotates by seat each round.
changes.why: Every seat now picks first twice, second twice, third twice and last twice, so the move-order edge disappears. The 3-player game stays at 12 rounds of 4 lots, already symmetric at 4 of each position.

changes.what: The Cats Favourite becomes +2 per fed cat, capped at +10.
changes.why: This removes the top end of the strongest Favourite: realistic value about +8-10.

changes.what: The Catnip Favourite becomes +2 per Catnip card owned (including any beyond 6), capped at +12.
changes.why: This raises the weakest Favourite. Catnip is heavily contested, and a holder typically gets 4-5 cards, so it is worth about +8-10.

changes.what: The Strays Favourite (4 players only) becomes +3 per Stray Cat. The Toys Favourite stays at +1 per Toy card.
changes.why: With about 6-7 Strays dealt across 8 rounds, a holder gets about 3, worth about +9. Toys is already about +8-10. All four Favourites now sit near +8-10, so the deal changes what to draft, not who leads.

Picks are sequential and public, so Favourites are already inferred from behaviour. Talk would add only cheap claims that cannot be checked, and no plan players could share, because every player competes for one win. It also costs steps.

keeps: Drafting groups of cards from a shared face-up market, with the cut-down market of 2-card lots from the previous variation
Cats must be fed: each needs 2 food, fed cats score 5, unfed cats score -1
Toy sets of Red, Blue and Green; the increasing catnip scale capped at 6 cards; Strays at 3 flat
The penalty for hoarding the most leftover food
Secret Favourites revealed at the end, inferred from picks
Highest total wins, tie-break most fed cats

recommendation.reason: The drafting core was balanced and reasoning-rich. Only the 4-player seat asymmetry and the Favourite spread needed fixing, and both fixes fit the limits.

variation.name: Cat Lady: Secret Favourites (Balanced)
variation.summary: Players draft 2-card lots from a public market, feeding cats, building toy sets, chasing catnip and collecting strays. Each player holds a secret Favourite that adds bonus points in one category. Seat order is fully symmetric, and the Favourites are tuned to be worth about the same.
variation.rules:
SETUP.
The deck has 96 cards:
- 18 Food-1 (1 food each)
- 10 Food-2 (2 food each)
- 20 Cat
- 8 Stray Cat
- 24 Toy (8 Red, 8 Blue, 8 Green)
- 16 Catnip
Shuffle the deck once.
Each player is secretly dealt one Favourite, and every player gets a different one. With 3 players the Favourites are drawn from {Cats, Toys, Catnip}; with 4 players they are drawn from {Cats, Toys, Catnip, Strays}. Only the owner knows their Favourite.
Seat the players in a fixed order, seat 1 to seat N.

ROUNDS.
With 3 players there are 12 rounds; with 4 players there are 8.
In round r, the first picker is seat ((r-1) mod N) + 1, and the others follow in seat order. Over the game, every seat holds each picking position equally often: 4 times each with 3 players, 2 times each with 4 players.

EACH ROUND.
1. Deal the market from the top of the deck. With 3 players deal 4 lots (Lot A to Lot D) of 2 cards each; with 4 players deal 5 lots (Lot A to Lot E) of 2 cards each. Announce every lot's contents to all players.
2. Starting with the first picker, each player in turn chooses one remaining lot by its letter. Each player sees all earlier picks.
3. A chosen lot goes to that player at once. Food cards add their food value to the player's food total. Cats, Strays, Toys (by colour) and Catnip are added to the player's counts. Everything a player owns is public, except their Favourite.
4. When every player has picked, the one leftover lot is discarded.
5. After the last round, go to final scoring. With 4 players, the 16 cards still in the deck are never used.

FINAL SCORING. For each player:
- Feeding: each Cat needs 2 food. Fed cats = the smaller of (Cats) and (food ÷ 2, rounded down). Each fed cat scores 5 and each unfed Cat scores -1. Leftover food = food total - 2 × fed cats.
- Strays: each Stray Cat scores 3.
- Toys: each Toy scores 1, plus 4 for each complete set of one Red, one Blue and one Green. Number of sets = the smallest of the three colour counts.
- Catnip: with n Catnip cards, counting at most 6, the player scores n(n+1)/2 (maximum 21). Catnip beyond 6 scores nothing here.
- Food penalty: the player or players with the most leftover food lose 2 points, provided that amount is at least 1.
- Favourite bonus, revealed now:
  - Cats: +2 per fed cat, maximum +10.
  - Toys: +1 per Toy card.
  - Catnip: +2 per Catnip card owned (including any beyond 6), maximum +12.
  - Strays (4 players only): +3 per Stray Cat.
variation.objective: The highest final total wins. If players are tied, the tied player with the most fed cats wins. If they are still tied, those players draw.
variation.expected_effect: With 8 rounds at 4 players, every seat picks first, second, third and last twice, so seat order no longer decides close games. Favourites now cluster around +8-10, so the secret deal mainly changes what each player should draft rather than who is ahead. Skill shows in planning food against cats, timing toy sets and the catnip curve, inferring rivals' Favourites from their picks, and denying key lots. No simple policy is safe. Fixed-letter picking accumulates unfed cats and the food penalty. Catnip-only play splits a contested suit and ignores Strays. Greedy points-now play misses feeding dependencies and denial. Talk is left out: every player competes for one win, picks already reveal intent, and claims about Favourites cannot be checked, so a discussion would add words, not reasoning.

balanced.evidence:
CARD VALUES (base, then with Favourite). Stray: 3 flat, needs nothing (5 with Strays fav). Catnip: marginal 1,2,3,4,5,6, so 6 cards = 21 (3.5/card); beyond 6 = 0 (+1/card with Catnip fav). Toy: 1/card + 4 per R/B/G set, so 3 cards = 7 (2.33/card; 3.33 with Toys fav). Cat: needs 2 food, fed = 5, unfed = -1. Cat + Food-2 = 5 for 2 cards (2.5/card); Cat + 2xFood-1 = 5 for 3 cards (1.67/card); with Cats fav 7. Food is scarce: total food = 18x1 + 10x2 = 38 against 20 Cats needing 40, so at most 19 fed cats exist. Card counts work out: 3p is 12 rounds x 8 = 96 (the whole deck); 4p is 9 x 10 = 90.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule). Lots are random 2-card bundles, so no lot letter is ever strictly better. 'Always earliest remaining letter' and 'always latest letter' each take an effectively random lot. Against a greedy drafter (best lot by the values above), they lose most games, because the greedy player completes catnip runs and toy sets while the fixed-letter player accumulates unfed cats (-1) and is likely to take the food penalty. They also give no edge against random play. 'Always most catnip': catnip's increasing marginal value makes it a commitment. Two chasers split 16 cards (about 8 each, with the last 2 worth 0), and the policy ignores Strays (3 flat), so it can be beaten. 'Always most points now' is not dominant either, because it ignores feeding dependencies and hate-drafting. There is no strictly dominant option and no never-lose policy, and every player can realistically win.

SEAT ORDER (fails). 3p: 12 rounds / 3 gives each seat 4 firsts, 4 seconds and 4 thirds, which is symmetric. 4p: 9 rounds is not divisible by 4. The first picker by round is S1, S2, S3, S4, S1, S2, S3, S4, S1, and the last picker is S4, S1, S2, S3, S4, S1, S2, S3, S4. So S1 picks first 3 times and last 2 times, while S4 picks first 2 times and last 3 times. Choosing first from 5 lots rather than last from 2 is worth roughly 2-4 points per round. In a game with totals around 40-60, a structural edge of about 4-8 points for S1 over S4 is a move-order edge built into the rules.

FAVOURITES. They are roughly comparable: Cats about +10-12 (5-6 fed cats), Toys about +8-10 (a category others value less), Catnip about +6-7 (heavily contested), Strays about +6-8 in 4p. They are not decisive, but Cats/Toys are somewhat stronger than Catnip.

playable.evidence:
The rules are complete. Setup, deck composition, lot dealing, pick order, card effects, the discard, and every scoring line (feeding with floor, unfed -1, the toy set formula, the catnip cap at 6, the food-penalty condition 'at least 1', favourite bonuses) are defined. The tie-break is fed cats, then a draw. The game is finite (12 or 9 rounds), and the deck covers every deal (96 or 90 of 96 cards). It is decided entirely by arithmetic on public counts plus one hidden attribute.

Limits: rounds 12 <= 40; choice steps 4 (one per picker) <= 4; hidden elements 2 (favourites, deck order) <= 3; random draws 1 (deck shuffled once, favourites dealt at setup) <= 1; attributes about 14 <= 20 (food, cats, strays, red, blue, green, catnip, favourite, plus lot slots). Steps 12 <= 20 is plausible: one multi-operation deal step with deck remove/append, announce, up to 4 pick steps that each apply the lot's increments, discard, and an end check. It is tight but feasible.

No board, clock, judge, trading or binding agreement is needed. Picks are sequential by design, and the order is the point of a draft.

Talk is absent, and that is acceptable here. Every pick is visible to later pickers, so nobody has to guess a simultaneous move. Talk would only add unenforceable claims about hidden Favourites.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance enters in two places: the lot contents (but the whole market is public before anyone picks) and the Favourite deal. Under equal good play, the outcome depends on reading the market: committing to catnip or toy sets early, pairing Cats with Food-2, avoiding being the leftover-food leader, and hate-drafting. I estimate chance at about 25-35% of the result, mostly from favourite asymmetry and from lots that happen to fall to whoever is next. That is not the sole decider: a favourite edge of about 4 points can be overcome by better drafting.

There is something to infer. Every holding is public except the Favourite, and opponents' picks reveal it. A player who repeatedly takes toys at a cost probably has the Toys favourite. With 3 or 4 favourites dealt without repetition, knowing your own leaves a small set of possibilities to narrow down. That inference can be acted on by denying key lots: taking the third colour of someone's set, or catnip from the player chasing 6. A planner who tracks remaining deck counts (for example 16 catnip, 8 strays, 38 food) is clearly favoured over one who picks the biggest-looking lot.

required_changes: Balanced: make the 4-player game a multiple of 4 rounds so every seat picks first, second, third and last equally often. Use 8 rounds of 5 lots (80 of 96 cards), or alternatively 12 rounds with 5 lots of 2 drawn from a 120-card deck scaled proportionally. Update stated complexity if rounds change.

Optional for balance: narrow the gap between Favourites, for example Catnip fav +2 per Catnip card beyond the 3rd, or Cats fav +2 per fed cat capped at 10, so that the random Favourite deal is closer to even.

balanced.evidence:
Value per card for a 3-player game (24 cards each):

| Card or combo | Base value | With matching Favourite |
|---|---|---|
| Cat + Food-2 (2 cards) | 5 (2.5/card) | 7 (3.5/card), Cats Favourite capped at +10 (5 fed cats) |
| Cat + Food-1 + Food-1 (3 cards) | 5 (1.67/card) | 7 (2.33/card) |
| Unfed Cat | -1 | -1 |
| Food-1 alone | 0 | 0 |
| Stray | 3 | 6 (4 players only) |
| Toy in a complete set | 1 + 4/3 = 2.33/card | 3.33/card, uncapped |
| Catnip, marginal 1st to 6th card | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (avg 3.5) | +2 each, capped at +12 (6 cards) |

No card type dominates. Catnip is strong only after investment and stops at 6 cards. Cats depend on contested food. Toys need all three colours. Value always depends on what a player already holds and what rivals take.

Realistic Favourite totals: Catnip specialist 6 Catnip = 21 + 12 = 33. Toys specialist 12 Toys in 4 sets = 12 + 16 + 12 = 40. Cats specialist 8 fed cats = 40 + 10 = 50, but this needs about 16 food. Each total leaves the player 6 to 18 cards for other scoring, so the Favourites are roughly comparable.

Thoughtless policies, judged by the winner rule:
- Always Lot A (first option): lot contents are random, so this is random play. A sensible drafter takes the best available lot for their holdings and outscores it in most games. It loses often and can only win on lucky deals.
- Always the last remaining lot: same result, random contents.
- Always the lot with the most food, or always Catnip: these overflow (food penalty -2, Catnip beyond 6 scores nothing) or starve cats (-1 each). Balanced drafters beat them.

No policy never loses, and no option is strictly better whatever opponents do.

Seat edge: the first picker rotates as ((r-1) mod N)+1. With 3 players, 12/3 gives each seat every picking position 4 times. With 4 players, 8/4 gives each position 2 times. Holdings are public apart from the Favourite, so no seat has an information edge.

There is no labelled payoff ordering to check. Every player can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
Card counts are exact. With 3 players, 12 rounds × 4 lots × 2 cards = 96, the whole deck. With 4 players, 8 × 5 × 2 = 80, leaving the stated 16 unused.

The rules cover every situation:
- Each pick is from the remaining lots and is sequential and visible, so the order is the point and turns are correct.
- The one leftover lot is discarded.
- Scoring formulas are explicit: fed cats = min(Cats, floor(food/2)); Catnip scores n(n+1)/2 with n capped at 6; toy sets = min of the three colour counts.
- The food penalty and tie-breaks are defined.
- 'Catnip Favourite: +2 per card including beyond 6, maximum +12' resolves arithmetically to min(2n, 12).

The game is finite (fixed rounds) and decided by arithmetic on kept counts. It needs no board, judge or real clock.

Complexity is within limits:
- steps_per_round 12 ≤ 20: deal, up to 4 picks, 4 resolutions, discard.
- choice_steps_per_round 4 ≤ 4: with 4 players exactly 4 picks; with 3 players, 3.
- attributes 15 ≤ 20: food, cats, strays, three toy colours, catnip, favourite, plus lot slots.
- hidden_elements 1 ≤ 3: the Favourite.
- random_draws_per_round 1: the market deal, using the shared-deck workaround.
- rounds 12 ≤ 40.

No talk with 3 to 4 players is acceptable. Players disagree over lots, but they act on each other's visible picks and public holdings, not blind guesses. Talk would mostly add cheap bluffing. This is not a fixed-length cooperation dilemma.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
Chance comes from the market deal and the random Favourite assignment. All players draft from the same public market, and picking positions are equalised by rotation, so a bad deal hits everyone. Favourite strengths are roughly comparable (estimated specialist totals of about 33 to 50 before the rest of the hand). I estimate chance decides roughly 25 to 35% of results.

There is a lot to reason about:
- Infer rivals' hidden Favourites from their picks; for example, someone taking a 4th Catnip early is probably the Catnip Favourite.
- Hate-draft lots a rival needs.
- Plan the food-to-cats ratio.
- Avoid the most-leftover-food penalty.
- Time when to complete toy sets.
- Use the known deck composition to predict what remains.

When all players draft well, the winner depends on how well each pursues their Favourite and denies others. That is not purely the deal, so a strong reasoner is clearly favoured.
